- Are you sure that it is the "wrong" page source? Google likely uses clientside code (JavaScript) to populate the character data once the page loads, i.e., the page source you receive won't look like the source of the browser because the source displayed in the browser has been changed by JavaScript after page load. `wget` and `curl` do not do any processing.

If you look at the wget log messages, you will see that you finally get "403 Forbidden" from Google.

So feel invited to look at [this Stackoverflow answer](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/29204103/wget-does-not-fetch-google-search-results#answer-29204186). Google doesn't want it's search results page to be used in an automated way, and I suppose they've got pretty good reasons.

If you want to do this anyway, you can set another User Agent string with `wget --user-agent=Chrome -O results.html 'https://www.google.com/search?hl=en&q=iron%20man%20character%20names'`

However, the answer you get from Google then is not easy to parse - maybe you can use a movie database for this task?

**wget is the wrong tool to download this page.**

The site uses a JavaScript framework, and it looks like the stylesheets are also loaded dynamically.

The actual content is only rendered and loaded at runtime via JavaScript.

`wget` fails because it only fetches static HTML and does not execute JavaScript, meaning it doesn’t run any scripts.

- [wget + JavaScript?](https://stackoverflow.com/q/5901661/12177498)

- [How do I use WGET so save this webpage](https://superuser.com/q/1554189/1780440)


Check out the source code and further details using the following methods (I did everything in Firefox):

##### 1\. Load/Open Page, than Right-click > "View Page Source"

This section shows that the content of the page is rendered and loaded ,in the body, inside:

`<plants-app></plants-app>`

```
<body>
  <plants-app></plants-app>
  <script src="polyfills-SIDVCFBP.js" type="module"></script>
  <script src="main-2UQUNJKT.js" type="module"></script>
</body>
</html>
```

##### 2\. Load/Open Page, than start the Web-Developer Tools, `F12` key.

You’ll see the fully rendered and loaded source code.

##### 3\. Load/Open Page, press `Ctrl` + `A` (to select all), than Right-click > "View Page Source" display the source code

You’ll see the fully rendered and loaded source code.

##### 4\. Load/Open Page, than load Page-Info, `Ctrl` + `I`

Under " **Media**", you can see all the paths to the images.

##### What you need are tools that emulate a browser.

They load the page, let it fully render, and then download the complete content.

**Check out these options:**

**Selenium** with python?

- [How to download a HTML webpage using Selenium with python?](https://stackoverflow.com/q/42900214/12177498)

**Puppeteer**

- [Puppeteer: how to download entire web page for offline use](https://stackoverflow.com/q/54814323/12177498)

**PhantomJS**

- [PhantomJS - Scriptable Headless Browser](https://phantomjs.org/)

**Playwright**

- [how to use playwright-python save web page to html or docx, txt, etc #435](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-python/issues/435)
- [How Do I Save a Complete Webpage to Read Offline Using Playwright \| Python](https://medium.com/@wisjnujudho/how-do-i-save-a-complete-webpage-to-read-offline-using-playwright-python-6dffadd8c9e5)

##### Custom Firefox/Chrome extension:

One option would be to create a Firefox/Chrome extension that automatically:

- Starts parsing from the index page

- Fully loads each page in the browser

- Completely saves the rendered content

- Then proceeds to the next link/page

- Repeats the process (load > save > next) recursively


##### Write your own parser/crawler

The final option would be that you write your own parser/crawler using a scripting language like Python or PHP, which, in combination with a browser, downloads the entire content of the domain.

This approach options would properly handle JavaScript-rendered content that tools like `wget` can't capture.

I finally did this...

First I acquired the list of all the plant name symbols: [https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/Txt/plantlst.txt](https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/Txt/plantlst.txt)

Then, I passed each symbol name one by one to playwright ( [https://pypi.org/project/playwright/](https://pypi.org/project/playwright/)) to launch a mini chromium browser to download the data.

```
import subprocess
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
from plant_ids import plant_ids
import time

def get_page(code, url, outfile):
  with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=True)  # Use headless=False to watch it
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto(url, wait_until="networkidle")
    page.pdf(path=outfile, format="A4")
    with open(f"./results/{code}.html", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
      f.write(page.content())
    browser.close()

sleep_time = 5

for code in plant_ids:
  print("plant code:",code)
  url = f"https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/{code}"
  outfile = f"./results/{code}.pdf"
  get_page(code, url, outfile)
  time.sleep(sleep_time)
  subprocess.run(["pdftotext", outfile, f"./results/{code}.txt"])

  print("plant code:",code,"images")
  url = f"https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/{code}/images"
  outfile = f"./results/{code}_images.pdf"
  get_page(code, url, outfile)
  time.sleep(sleep_time)
  subprocess.run(["pdfimages", "-png", outfile, f"./results/{code}_image"])

  print("plant code:",code,"synonyms")
  url = f"https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/{code}/synonyms"
  outfile = f"./results/{code}_synonyms.pdf"
  get_page(code, url, outfile)
  time.sleep(sleep_time)

  print("plant code:",code,"related-links")
  url = f"https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/{code}/related-links"
  print("plant code:",code,"related-links")
  outfile = f"./results/{code}_related.pdf"
  get_page(code, url, outfile)
  time.sleep(sleep_time)
```

cURL and wget are used to **transfer** files/content to/from a specified location. As such, cURL and wget are neither suitable for actually rendering web pages nor executing JavaScript on those webpages. While cURL can be used to output received data to stdout, it is still not designed to render that data.

If you would like to use the terminal to execute JavaScript within a webpage, you may want to consider looking into [PhantomJS](http://phantomjs.org/). PhantomJS can load local HTML files and interact with/execute their JavaScript.

If you just want to call a PHP script you can do:

```
curl http://your-domain.com/script.php
```

But with just wget your script will be downloaded:

```
wget http://your-domain.com/script.php
```

But with wget -q -O you can call the script like curl:

```
wget -q -O http://your-domain.com/script.php
```

I have tried `wget -m``wget -r` and a whole bunch of variations. I am getting some of the images on [http://site.com](http://site.com/), one of the scripts, and none of the CSS, even with the fscking `-p` parameter. The only HTML page is index.html and there are several more referenced, so I am at a loss. `curlmirror.pl` on the cURL developers website does not seem to get the job done either. Is there something I am missing? I have tried different levels of recursion with only this URL, but I get the feeling I am missing something. Long story short, some school allows its students to submit web projects, but they want to know how they can collect everything for the instructor who will grade it, instead of him going to all the externally hsoted sites.

**UPDATE**: I think I figured out the issue. I though the links to the other pages were in the index.html page that downloaded. I was _way_ off. Turns out the footer of the page, which has all the navigation links, is handled by a JavaScript file `Include.js`, which reads `JLSSiteMap.js` and some other JS files to do page navigation and the like. As a result, wget does not pick up an other dependencies because a lot of this crap is handled not on web pages. How can I handle such a website? This is one of several problem cases. I assume little can be done if wget cannot parse JavaScript.

Unfortunately wget cannot parse JavaScript, so spidering such a site is quite difficult.

The good news is, [search engines don't generally parse it either](http://googlewebmastercentral.blogspot.com/2007/11/spiders-view-of-web-20.html), so they are most likely feeding slightly different content to search engines (which is a bad idea for [other reasons](http://support.google.com/webmasters/bin/answer.py?hl=en&answer=66355)) so that they can get their pages indexed. They have to feed search engines pages which are reachable without JavaScript if they want to actually be indexed. If this is the case, you can work around it by spoofing Googlebot with wget, such as:

```
wget --user-agent="Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Googlebot/2.1; +http://www. google.com/bot.html)" ...
```

A very few sites will actually check your IP address to see if you're really Googlebot, but this is far less common than it should be.

Another thing to do is to check for the presence of a `/sitemap.xml` file and use it as a list of URLs to crawl. Some sites provide this file [for Google and other search engines to use](https://support.google.com/webmasters/bin/answer.py?hl=en&answer=156184) to spider their content, but nothing says you can't also use it...
